## Original Research

The utility of the 5-Item frailty index in assessing the risk of complications and mortality following surgical management of non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage

Qais AbuHasan a,b,*

, Jakob V.E. Gerstl b, Chady Omara b,c, Harshit Arora b, Muhieddine Labban d, Abdullah H. Feroze b, Timothy R. Smith b, Mohammad A. Aziz-Sultan b

a Department of Neurology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School Boston MA United States of America b Computational Neuroscience Outcomes Center, Department of Neurosurgery, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School Boston MA United States of America c Department of Neurosurgery Leiden University Medical Center (LUMC) Leiden the Netherlands d Division of Urological Surgery, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School Boston MA United States of America

A R T I C L E  I N F O

Keywords: Complications Frailty Mortality Subarachnoid hemorrhage

A B S T R A C T

The modified 5-item frailty index (mFI-5), an index of reduced physiological reserve, has risen as a predictor of complications following surgical procedures. We examined the association of mFI-5 and surgical outcomes following the management of nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (nSAH). We queried the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database for patients who received surgical man­ agement of nSAH between 2006 and 2021. We computed the mFI-5 by granting a point for each of 1) congestive heart failure, 2) hypertension requiring medications, 3) diabetes, 4) chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or pneumonia within 30 days before surgery, and 5) dependent functional status. Our 30-day endpoints were minor complications (Clavien-Dindo: 1 & 2), major complications (Clavien-Dindo: 3 & 4), and mortality. Using the Chisquared test, we compared baseline patient demographics and comorbidities between patients with a mFI-5 ≥2, patients with a mFI-5 = 1, and non-frail patients. Then, we fitted a multivariable logistic regression adjusting for patient demographics, comorbidities, operative time, and frailty status. The cohort included 1,139 patients, of which 33.7 % were men and 2.9 % had a bleeding diathesis. After adjusting for covariates, mFI-5 ≥2 was independently associated with minor complications (1.93, 95 %CI: 1.31–2.84, p = 0.001), major complications (aOR: 1.62, 95 %CI: 1.10–2.37, p = 0.015), and mortality (aOR: 2.90, 95 %CI: 1.66–5.08, p = 0.003). The mFI-5 can be independently used by surgeons for risk stratification and postoperative planning.

## 1. Introduction

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) has a worldwide incidence of 7.9 per 100,000 person-years with high morbidity and mortality rates [1,2]. It is most often caused by the rupture of brain aneurysms and less commonly due to arterio-venous malformation (AVM), among other etiologies [3,4]. The most widely used treatment modalities include aneurysmal clipping and endovascular coiling [5]. Due to the increased incidence of SAH among older patients, these procedures are often performed among frail patients [6]. It has been reported that 25–45 % of patients with SAH are frail and are at increased risk for developing poor health outcomes following surgery [7–10]. Therefore, it is important to

assess the frailty of patients with SAH to gain better insight into preoperative risk assessment and advanced care planning.

Frailty reflects increased vulnerability to stressors and decreased physiological reserve [11]. It is associated with age-related declines across multiple physiological systems and, due to the aging population, has been gaining more prominence in decision-making within health­ care [12,13]. The effect of frailty on peri-operative and long-term com­ plications, as well as mortality, has been investigated in various surgical fields [14–16]. Recent studies have demonstrated that frailty can be utilized as an independent determinant of poor health outcomes and that frail adults are less able to tolerate stressors such as medical in­ terventions or surgery [12,17].

Within neurosurgery, the association between frailty and outcomes has been explored using different frailty measures [18,19]. In patients with SAH, frailty assessed by the Johns Hopkins Adjusted Clinical Groups frailty indicator (ACG) was significantly associated with an increased risk of postoperative complications and a reduced risk of inhospital mortality [20]. The modified 5-item frailty index (mFI-5) is a comorbidity-based tool designed to stratify patients based on the level of frailty, which has been used among several neurosurgical procedures [21]. It is a simple method that has recently gained traction to evaluate frailty among surgical patients but has yet to be evaluated thoroughly among patients with nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (nSAH). In this study, we sought to examine the utility of mFI-5 in assessing the risk of complications and mortality following the surgical management of nSAH using a large national database.

## 2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Data Source

We queried the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (ACS NSQIP) database, which is an initiative that systematically collects and analyzes patient data and evaluates surgical outcomes up to 30 days following the procedure on a national scale. We included patients who had a primary diagnosis of nSAH between 2006 and 2021 using the ICD9 code “430” and the ICD10 code “I60” and its sub-specifiers. Patients who received surgical man­ agement for aneurysms or arterio-venous malformations were included using the current procedural terminology (CPT) codes: 61680, 61682, 61684, 61686, 61697, 61698, 61700, 61702, 61703, 61,705 (Appendix 1).

2.2. Exposure

The frailty score was calculated as previously described [22]. One point was given for each of 1) congestive heart failure, 2) hypertension requiring medications, 3) diabetes mellitus requiring treatment with oral agents or insulin, 4) chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or pneumonia within 30 days before surgery, and 5) dependent func­ tional status (total or partial inability to perform activities of daily living). Patients were categorized into three groups based on the mFI-5; non-frail patients (mFI-5 = 0), frail patients with mFI-5 = 1, and frail patients with mFI-5 ≥2 as previously reported in the literature [21].

2.3. Endpoints

The 30-day outcomes were defined as outcomes occurring within 30 days following index surgery. The 30-day complications were catego­ rized into minor and major complications according to the Clavien-

Dindo (CD) classification as defined in Table 1 [23]. Postoperative complications falling into Clavien-Dindo grades 1 and 2 were defined as minor complications, while Clavien-Dindo classifications 3 and 4 were defined as major complications. The 30-day mortality was also recorded.

2.4. Covariates

Patient demographics were recorded, including age, sex, and race. Other variables included obesity, defined as BMI ≥30, smoking status, presence of a bleeding diathesis, chronic use of corticosteroids for medical conditions, American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) clas­ sification, operative time, and the year of the operation.

2.5. Statistical analysis

We compared demographics, comorbidities, perioperative factors, and outcomes between frailty groups using the Chi-squared test. Then, we fitted separate multivariable logistic regressions adjusting for patient demographics, comorbidities, ASA class, and perioperative factors to examine the independent association between mFI-5 and the surgical outcomes, including minor complications, major complications, and mortality. Those factors have been described in the literature to be associated with surgical outcomes. A similar multivariable logistic regression model was fitted to assess the association of mFI-5 with complications categorized into medical and surgical complications. Additionally, a separate model was used to assess the association of each of the mFI-5 components with the outcomes of interest. No collinearity was detected in the primary regression models. However, collinearity was detected in 3 out of 9 models that assess the association between frailty and outcomes stratified by age. In these models, chronic steroid use and/or bleeding diatheses exhibited collinearity and were dropped from the models. Subsequently, 3–4 observations were dropped from the analysis. The adjusted odds ratios (aOR) and the corresponding 95 % confidence intervals (95 % CI) were reported.

Statistical analyses were performed using STATA 17 (StataCorp, Texas, USA). Statistical significance was set at a two-sided p-value < 0.05. Because NSQIP is a de-identified registry, this work does not involve human subject research; therefore, institutional review board was exempt.

## 3. Results

A total of 1,139 patients were included. Of those, 1,008 (88.5 %) underwent aneurysmal repair while 99 (8.7 %) had an AV malformation repair and 32 (2.8 %) had other repairs. Patients were classified ac­ cording to mFI-5; score = 0 (n = 557; 48.9 %), score = 1 (n = 415; 36.4 %) and score ≥2 (n = 167; 14.7 %). Frail patients with a mFI-5 score ≥2 were more likely to be older, have obesity, have a bleeding diathesis, and use corticosteroids chronically (p < 0.003 for corticosteroid use and p < 0.001 for the rest; Table 2). Patients with a mFI-5 score ≥2 were more likely to encounter minor complications compared to non-frail patients and patients with a mFI-5 score = 1 (50.3 % vs. 29.8 % and 37.6 %, p < 0.001), major complications (57.5 % vs. 37.7 % and 48.0 %, p < 0.001), and higher mortality (21.0 % vs. 6.3 % and 14.2 %, p < 0.001).

In the adjusted analysis, frailty with mFI-5 ≥2 was associated with increased minor complications (aOR: 1.93, 95% CI: 1.31–2.84, p = 0.001), major complications (aOR: 1.62, 95% CI: 1.10–2.37, p = 0.015), and mortality (aOR: 2.90, 95% CI: 1.66–5.08, p < 0.001). Patients with a mFI-5 = 1 had significantly higher odds of mortality (aOR: 2.04, 95% CI: 1.28–3.26, p = 0.003), while no significant difference in odds of minor or major complications was found compared to the patients with mFI-5 score of 0 (Table 3). Additionally, mFI-5 ≥2 was associated with increased medical complications (aOR: 1.78, 95% CI: 1.19–2.65, p = 0.005), and increased surgical complications (aOR: 1.54, 95% CI: 1.04–2.27, p = 0.030). When stratifying according to age, mFI-5 ≥2 in patients younger than 50 years was associated with higher minor complications (aOR: 2.38, 95% CI: 1.08–5.26, p = 0.032) and major complications (aOR: 3.36, 95% CI: 1.50–7.53, p = 0.003) compared to patients with mFI-5 score of 0 (Table 4). Frailty was not associated with mortality in younger patients. However, patients ≥60 years with mFI-5 ≥2 had higher odds of mortality compared to patients with an mFI-5 of 0 (aOR: 6.65, 95% CI: 2.53–17.49, p < 0.001).

When assessing the components of mFI-5 independently, COPD or pneumonia was associated with increased odds of minor complications (aOR: 3.38, 95% CI: 2.06–5.54, p < 0.001), major complications (aOR: 2.61, 95% CI: 1.58–4.32, p < 0.001), and mortality (aOR: 2.90, 95% CI: 1.64–5.14, p < 0.001). Similarly, patients with a dependent functional status had higher minor complications (aOR: 2.51, 95% CI: 1.62–3.90, p < 0.001), major complications (aOR: 2.41, 95% CI: 1.54–3.77, p < 0.001), and mortality (aOR: 2.26, 95% CI: 1.27–4.00, p = 0.005).

## 4. Discussion

Our national database analysis showed that frailty assessed by mFI-5 is independently associated with surgical outcomes. Patients with a mFI- 5 of 2 or more have increased odds of developing postoperative minor and major complications and higher mortality within 30 days of surgical management of nSAH. The mFI-5 could be used as a tool to assess pa­ tients’ risk for developing postoperative complications and mortality.

Various tools measuring frailty have been used in the literature across surgical specialties to predict surgical complications and out­ comes [24–26]. The modified frailty index 11 (mFI-11) has been used in studies using the NSQIP database, and its derivative, the mFI-5, is taking its place as an equally useful tool because of its practicality in the clinical setting [21,22]. Another national study used the National Inpatient Sample to study postoperative outcomes among patients with aneu­ rysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) and found that frailty measured using the Johns Hopkins Adjusted Clinical Groups was an independent predictor of surgical complications [20]. However, findings are conflicting across single-center studies. For instance, McIntyre et al. found that the mFI-11 can predict outcomes in angiogram-negative subarachnoid hemorrhage [27], while Lim et al. used the mFI-5 among patients with aSAH and found that it does not predict surgical outcomes [28]. Our analysis of the NSQIP demonstrated that frail pa­ tients have an increased risk of developing complications regardless of their severity, ranging from easily managed symptoms to complications requiring ICU admission or reoperation. While the ASA classification was associated with increased complications and mortality as previously reported [29], frailty had an independent association with complica­ tions and mortality regardless of the ASA classification.

Moreover, frailty could predict early mortality following surgical treatment of nSAH. We found that frail patients in both frailty categories had higher odds of mortality within 30 days of index surgery. In contrast, a previous analysis of the NIS dataset showed that frailty re­ duces the risk of in-hospital mortality [20]. McIntyre et al. reported age as the determinant of mortality rather than frailty in aSAH [9]. How­ ever, they found that, compared to age, frailty was a superior predictor of mortality among patients with angiogram-negative SAH [27]. This suggests that frailty as a risk factor could be diagnosis-specific, war­ ranting further investigative efforts to assess its utility in different pathologies.

The limitations of this study pertain mainly to the shortcomings of using the ACS NSQIP database. The study design is retrospective and can establish an association rather than a causality relationship. Addition­ ally, despite the large number of participating hospitals, the generaliz­ ability could be affected as the infrastructure required for the data collection could not be readily available for smaller hospitals. The standardized data collection procedure does not include specific neurosurgical information. As a result, we could not compare treatment modalities for SAH (e.g., endovascular coiling vs. clipping), isolate specific etiologies of nSAH (aneurysms, AV malformations, and other causes that may have different presentations, management, and prog­ nosis that are not fully captured using the CPT codes), or account for the clinical grade of the hemorrhage using the WFNS or other grading sys­ tems. Despite these limitations, this analysis provides a comprehensive review of the utility of the mFI-5 in assessing the 30-day outcomes in patients with nSAH.

## 5. Conclusion

The mFI-5 could be used to predict postoperative complications and mortality following nSAH independently. Our work suggests that the assessment of frailty may provide valuable information for routine preoperative risk evaluation, particularly for younger patients. Accordingly, further attention can be mobilized to care for this vulner­ able patient population to optimize postoperative care plans to reduce

complications and mortality.
